en: Preface to the Recorded Sayings of Wujia:
Prior to the time of King Vairocana (Viyūnaprabha), there appeared immeasurable Buddhas and patriarchs, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.

Taking the worlds of the ten directions as their mouths, they uttered immeasurable words and discoursed upon immeasurable subtle meanings; yet people of that time still clung to the [physical marks of] the thirty-two [major characteristics].
His voice was like that of the kalaviṅka bird; as he was the true Dharma-body of a Buddha, his manifestations were inexhaustible.
Together they entered the fire-altar of transformation, each leaving behind eight *hu* and four *dou* of relics, which the Wheel-Turning King collected and used to construct a nine-storied stūpa.

Reaching the ninth tier, at the summit where one cannot proceed further, a *candana* sandalwood pillar—measuring a thousand *zhang* in height and several hundred *wei* in girth—is brought down from the void by means of a drill.
From the intersecting corners of the pagoda’s structure, it penetrates from top to bottom, standing loftily beyond the ordinary.
Above it are successive tiers of precious discs; rising higher still, there is a sharp, pointed golden pinnacle that extends upward beyond the crown.

In emptiness, five-colored jewel-radiance surged forth. From each and every ray of light, there appeared forms that were neither blue nor yellow, neither red, white, nor black—distinctly clear yet beyond the conceptualization of separate parts.
This caused the person to count the layers to their end and peer through to the very peak, discerning the five lights until the pathways of the conscious mind were severed.
Unknowingly and unawares, the eyes grew dizzy and the ears rang with a thunderous roar.

Yet, when the thunderbolt shattered his crown, his entire body transformed into the light of *śarīra*, which remained throughout the day within the vast void as an auspicious omen and a portent, appearing and disappearing at will.
It caused all sentient beings who saw or heard it to enter together into the *pañca-raśmi-samādhi*.
Indeed, this teaching of the present era is the direct lineage of the five houses of Zen; for what reason? Because [it] honors...
The nine-story height represents the doctrinal meaning of the teachings of the five periods; it is that which the human mind can reach and upon which one can rely for practice.
The summit where they are joined refers to the fourfold binding of Tathāgata-dhyāna;

it is a place where the Buddhas of the three ages hang their mouths upon the wall, and where even those of great intelligence find their minds as still as wood or stone. The thousand-fathom sandalwood tree breaking through the summit from the void signifies this.
The Zen of the Patriarchs turns beyond the extraordinary; it overturns the old molds, being direct and incisive—this is it.
Upon a layered jeweled platter stands a golden pinnacle; as it turns, it rises higher, becoming ever more refined and sharp—this is it.
This is the very face seen by each of the two lineages, from Kāśyapa’s breaking into a smile down to the Sixth Patriarch. Departing from the pinnacle, one enters the void.
The emission of five-colored light refers to the division into five schools, each establishing its own fundamental tenets.

That these five colors are not blue, yellow, red, white, or black, yet are vividly clear and cannot be categorized by class, signifies the very face and character of the essential principles of each of the five houses.
It causes people to see through to the ultimate level of the teachings and the pinnacle of the school, until the mind is stilled and hearing ceases like the fading of thunder.
It transforms into the light of the *śarīra* relics throughout the entire body, serving as an auspicious omen and a portent within the great void.

Appearing and disappearing at times, it causes all sentient beings who see or hear it to enter the *pañca-raśmi-samādhi*, to enter the inconceivable realm, and to attain great mastery—entering the domain where both Māras and Buddhas abide.
This is why these five schools are considered the most supreme among all doctrinal schools.

This is the causal condition for the one great matter. Those who are now disciples of the Buddha, when entering the Teachings (Dharmavinaya), cannot transcend the nine grades and penetrate the summit of the knots;
when entering the School (Zong), they are limited by the "drilling wood" and lack the "heavy platter.
Thus, upon hearing of the five lights, they all respond with anger and abuse, laughing and spitting, saying: "What use has he for these lights if he does not possess form?"

Furthermore, it would not be strange or demonic that my body and mind were shattered. Thus, those skilled in eloquent speech prize rapidity, while those skilled in practical application value independence and firmness.
Consequently, the five schools came to be regarded as derivative branches, while the core tenets were treated as mere scholastic studies.
Carve up the pears; pare away the words. Let the true descendants of Linji, Yunmen, Guiyang, Fayan, and Caodong have their heads split and their brains shattered.
Strive to ensure that the Dharma is free from restraint and that the Way may be transmitted in a barbarian fashion.

Only when the descendants fill the world and the five houses have been wiped out will this be a truly great joy. What need is there for Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa anymore? Why should one make vows to appear again?
He who has come to uphold the true lineage during the Final Dharma is the layman Li Jian of Haichang. Having sought the Way for a long time, his entry into the Dharma has grown ever deeper.
He regards the salvation of the Dharma as urgent as saving his own head on fire, and his protection of the world as vital as guarding his own eyes.

He has searched through the recorded sayings of the Five Houses and carved them into woodblocks to disseminate them widely throughout Jambudvīpa, so that all those in the world with eyes may behold the pinnacle of the stupa.
The body of the Buddha Emitting Light (Prabhūtaratna) is eternally present; those whose eyes enter [this space] all attain the Samādhi of Spontaneous Freedom in the Five Radiances.
This layman’s merit is effortless—how could it be measured by the merits of a Buddhist stupa?
At my request for a preface, I am ashamed that I cannot elucidate the true intent of the five schools; I shall merely add a handful of sand upon the summit of this stupa.

Do not allow others to further pursue the five lights; do not discriminate between the non-existent and the existent, nor argue for what is right and what is wrong, lest you lose both eyes of discernment.
Written with prostrations by He-nan of Mi-fa-zang at Tianshou Sheng’en Chan Monastery on Mount Wei in Deng, Wu Gate.
*The Chart of the Source and Lineage of the Five Schools*
The First Patriarch of the Eastern Land, Bodhidharma;
the Second Patriarch, Huike;
and the Third Patriarch, Sengcan.
The Fourth Patriarch Daoxin,
the Fifth Patriarch Hongren,
and the Sixth Patriarch Huineng.
(Dajian) Huineng (1st generation), Nanyue Huairang (2nd generation),
Mazu Daoyi (3rd generation), Baizhang Huaihai.
(4th generation) Huangbo Xiyun;
(5th generation) Linji Yixuan and Muzhou Daoyou.
Yangshan Ji (3rd generation), Tianwang Wu (4th generation), Longtan Xin.
(5th generation) Deshan Jian;
(6th generation) Xuefeng Cun;
(7th generation) Yunmen Wenyan.
Xuansha Bei (8th generation),
Luohan Chen (9th generation), and Qingliang Yi.
(Dajian Huineng, 1st generation) Qingyuan Xingsi (2nd generation) Shitou Xiqian (3rd generation) Yaoshan Weiyan.
(4th generation) Yunyan Cheng;
(5th generation) Dongshan Jia;
(6th generation) Caoshan Benji.

Since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, he transmitted the Dharma to the Second Patriarch; the Second Patriarch transmitted it to the Third Patriarch; the Third Patriarch to the Fourth Patriarch; the Fourth Patriarch to the Fifth Patriarch;
and the Fifth Patriarch to the Sixth Patriarch. The Sixth Patriarch subsequently gave rise to the two schools of Nanyue and Qingyuan.
From Nanyue came Mazu Daoyi, and from Daoyi came Baizhang Huaihai. From Huaihai came Huangbo Xiyun, and from Xiyun came Linji Yixuan.
He established the orthodox lineage, thereby forming the Linji school. Following Mazu, Huishan Daoyou appeared; Daoyou received Xuefeng Yicun, who in turn received Yangshan Huiji.
Together they sang and responded in verse, forming the Weiyang school. Subsequently, Qingyuan Xingsi gave rise to Shitou Xiqian, and Xiqian gave rise to Yaoshan Weiyan.
Yan emerged from Yunyan Tancheng; Cheng emerged from Dongshan Liangjie; and Jia obtained Cao Shan Benji, thereby establishing the Caodong school.
From Mazu Daoyi, Tianwang Baoji emerged next; Wu emerged from Longtan Chongxin; Xin emerged from Deshan Xuanjian; Jian emerged from Xuefeng Yicun;
Cun obtained Yunmen Wenyan, thereby establishing the Yunmen school. Following Cun, Xuansha Shibei emerged; Bei emerged from Luohan Guichen.

Chen. Chen attained the benefit of "cooling" (liberation) and established the Fa-yen school. However, regarding the two schools of Yun-men and Fa-yen, the *Jingde Chuandeng Lu* erroneously places them under Qing-yuan.
According to the *Epitaph for Chan Master Xue-du Xian*, they are described as the ninth-generation descendants of Mazu Da-jì.
Tracing back further, Xue-du succeeded Zhi-men Zu; Zu succeeded Xiang-lin Yuan; and Yuan succeeded... [text continues]
Xuefeng Cun. Since Yunmen succeeded Xuefeng and Xuansha also succeeded Xuefeng, it is beyond doubt that both lineages belong to Master Mazu.
During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Rui of Yuyao Yunhe compiled the *Xindeng Lu* (Record of the Lamp of the Mind), in which he likewise classified both lineages as branches of the Nanyue school.
Few in the world were aware of this, as the work did not circulate widely; this was likely because of the times.
Lacking the discerning hand and eye, people have followed errors and perpetuated corruptions without correcting one another.

Now, having examined the *Wudeng Huiyuan*, I find that following the "Transmission of Enlightenment by Tianwang," its account is recorded in detail; the sources and lineages are synthesized and analyzed with clarity.

When verified against the views of the venerable masters Jin-su, Wu Jing-shan, Xin Zhen-ji, and Yin, they all concur with this perspective. Thus, I have composed this "Source and Lineage of the Five Houses."
Diagram. After this transmission has been revised and finalized, those who possess the discerning eye of the Dharma should verify it for themselves.
Preface to the Recorded Sayings of the Five Houses.

Regarding the recorded sayings of the Five Houses: from the time Bodhidharma came from the West until the sixth generation, spanning four successive patriarchates, the Dharma spread throughout China. Zen...

Equipped with all essential elements, their pedagogical expressions varied; though they were undifferentiated in their mindlessness, they naturally formed five schools—namely, Wei, Yang, Linji, Caodong, Yunmen, and Fayan.
Although these five schools differ in their functional applications, none deviate from the fundamental principle of direct pointing.
Now, Layman Líméi has carved this record of sayings and further established a formal diagram based on the words of former masters who provided verification and clarification.
This may be called "receiving from above and initiating below," encompassing both the past and the present.

Those who read these records can exhaustively grasp the fundamental principles of the Five Houses' distinctions, thereby clarifying the wisdom of their own particular differentiation. All of this ultimately returns to the local scenery of one's own original ground. Complete.
The great functioning of the pivot lies beyond the realm of words and letters;

thus, even if the descendants of the Five Houses, the empty-headed disciples of the Buddha-king, or even foxes, wolves, and jackals should arrive, he gives them all thirty blows of the staff. Why is this so?
To let this pass here would be unacceptable.
Written and calligraphed by Míyún Yuánwù at the abbot’s quarters of Mount Tiantong during the first month of spring in the *rénshēn* year of the Chóngzhēn era (1632).
Preface to the *Wǔjiā Yŭlù*.
The World-Honored One was on Mount Snowy (Himavat). Upon beholding the morning star, he attained great enlightenment and sighed, saying: "How marvelous!
All sentient beings are fully endowed with the wisdom, virtue, and marks of the Tathāgata; yet, due to deluded thoughts and attachments, they do not realize it.

The entanglements of the twelve divisions of the scriptures originate from this point. As for pointing directly at the human mind, they have not yet even reached it. Only Bodhidharma is still superior."
A mere trifle. Lightly carrying a single bowl, he passed through my land of China. This "special transmission outside the teachings" was intended to receive those of the highest capacity;

yet, upon meeting an incompetent fellow at the very outset, he shook his sleeves and retired to a deserted mountain to sit in cold meditation for nine years. Later, he obtained Huikě to continue the life of wisdom.
Thus, through successive transmission and reception, it reached the Sixth Patriarch Dajian, at which point the robe and bowl were no longer passed on, and his Dharma alone was transmitted. One.
Is this not what was meant by the prophecy that "the flower would bloom in five petals"? Under the Sixth Patriarch, two branches emerged: Nanyue Huairang and Qingyuan Xingsi.
From Nanyue descended the lineages of Guishan Lingyou, Yangshan Huiji, Linji Yixuan, Yunmen Wenyan, and Fayan Wenyi. From Qingyuan descended the lineage of Caodong.
The masters of Miu and Yang, father and son, possessed ninety-seven kinds of circular diagrams (*yuánxiàng*), utilizing golden needles and jade threads.

Linji had the four guest-host relationships, the four methods of selection, and the three shouts and three mysteries-three essentials (*sān xuán sān yào*). Within a single phrase are contained the three mysteries; within each mystery are contained the three essentials.

To possess both the mysteries and the essentials is the fundamental principle of our school. It is by means of this that we establish the banner of the Dharma and loftily uphold the patriarchal style.
The Tuṣita Heaven was thrown into turmoil; stars flew and constellations scattered. Linji’s radiance was so brilliant and crimson that no one dared look directly at him.

As he was about to manifest his passing, he spoke this verse on the transmission of the Dharma: "Following the current without ceasing—ask how it is? True illumination is boundless—explain it to others thus.
Free from characteristics and free from names, no one receives it; Having used the 'blow-off-blade,' one must immediately polish it. Following the current without ceasing...

A single phrase [suffices] to prophesy that the source and stream [of this lineage] will endure for a long time. As for the other three schools—Guiyang, Yunmen, and Fayan—they have long since vanished;
though their lineages nominally exist, they lack the true masters to sustain them. As for the Caodong school, it seems to exist only as a faint echo or shadow.
Half is similar and half is not. If it were like ice-moons or frost-flowers, then the west wind would surely sweep them from the ground.
During the Song dynasty, Chan Master Dahui Zonggao was a peerless figure among all quarters; wielding the sword that governs both killing and giving life, he revived the spirit of Linji.

Upon hearing thunder, those who had committed the five rebellious acts realized the truth for themselves without the need for words. In recent times, the Way has become shallow and the time has grown arid; people mistake mere dryness and barrenness for Chan. Never...
They have not heard of the marvels of the Blood-Basin Mouth or the Sky-Scratching Talented Hawks;
they do not employ the staff or the shout, nor do they transcend the insights of the ancients. Regarding the mechanism of life and death, there is not a single word.

It is not that they are incapable, but rather that they have not reached the state of vast, boundless openness. Since they remain in a realm of shallow shores and boundaries, their very life-root has never been severed.

Sever it! How can one hope to be like the ancients? When starlight fills the four fields and moonlight pervades the heavens, there is a solitary brilliance such that no body of water fails to reflect it;
whether to the left or to the right, nothing is not fully prepared. Alas! People today possess the awakening of empty fame but lack the merit of actual realization.
Their functional application is not even comparable; they are as far apart as heaven and earth. As the Zen school declines, there is only a chirping clamor of confusion.
Weeping, as his life comes to an end in darkness, he does not pass from the hands of an ordinary person; when habitual tendencies manifest, it is difficult to escape the barrier of birth and death.

One must be like the ancient masters who, ascending the hall, announced their passing and returned home with ease. I fear that even after as many donkey years as it takes to dream of this, you have not yet glimpsed it.
Layman Limui of Haichang has long devoted himself to this Way; he has not shunned hardship in his travels to seek out teachers and gain realization.
The consciousness has grasped it and returned; one may enjoy it as one pleases.

Possessing the eye of discernment and prepared with the skill of both concession and withdrawal, when encountering a person of middle capacity, one reveals a word or half a phrase—like jade within stone. How could an ordinary person easily know this?
I have searched through the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of five venerable patriarchs, compiled them into this volume, and carved it for publication so that it may endure imperishably.
May those who see or hear it awaken to the wisdom of past lives and realize that there exists a True Person beyond rank, free from form and name, who points toward the ultimate transcendence.
Not treading the winding paths of birth and death, he strides high upon the crowns of the patriarchs and Buddhas. The Treasury of the True Dharma Eye is about to be revealed;
when the Buddha of the Empty King appears, how will you deliberate? What about this fellow from the fields?
Composed and calligraphed by the Śramaṇa Yufeng Yuanxin of Mount Jing during the winter of the Gengwu year of the Chongzhen era.
